name: Wotu
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: 9. Klemtoon. In het Sada'sch en Wotoe'sch valt de klemtoon zooals die thans bij de meeste Indonesische talen valt: op de voorlaatste lettergreep, zoowel bij stamwoorden als bij afgeleide woorden. De suffixen worden voor den klemtoon als laatste lettergrepen van het woord waaraan zij gehecht zijn, beschouwd. [...] In het Wotu'sch schijnt een oxytonisch accent intusschen niet ongewoon te zijn. De Wdl., die toch slechts een klein deel van den woordenschat omvat, geeft er een aantal voorbeelden van. Zij zijn: aró „borst" (Bug. aro „lichaam"); ranrá „maagd", (Sad. Bug. dara); mitjú „spuwen" (Bug. mamitju); tobó „dolk" (Sad. Mak. Bug. tobo); [...] mabaló „fraai" [...]; mawarú „nieuw".
new_statements.translation: 9. Stress. In Sada and Wotu the stress falls as it now falls in most Indonesian languages: on the penultimate syllable, both in stem words and in derived words. For the purposes of stress the suffixes are regarded as final syllables of the word to which they are attached. [...] In Wotu, however, an oxytone accent seems not to be unusual. The wordlist, which after all covers only a small part of the vocabulary, gives a number of examples of it. They are: aró 'chest' (Bug. aro 'body'); ranrá 'maiden' (Sad. Bug. dara); mitjú 'spit' (Bug. mamitju); tobó 'dagger' (Sad. Mak. Bug. tobo); [...] mabaló 'fine, beautiful' [...]; mawarú 'new'.
new_statements.citation: Adriani, N. 1898. Iets over de talen der To Sada en der To Wadu. Mededeelingen van wege het Nederlandsche Zendelinggenootschap 42 (running head 'MED. N.Z.G. XLII'; Mead 2013 cites it as vol. 41): 111-150.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Checked the held scan (608 pp., no text layer) by rendering PDF pages 119, 126 and 127 at 110 dpi and reading the page images, plus the IA scanned text ( lines 5288-5326). Page 126 carries printed page number 118 and, at the foot of the previous paragraph 8, the heading '9. Klemtoon. In het Sada'sch en Wotoe'sch valt de klemtoon zooals die thans bij de meeste Indonesische talen valt: op de voorlaatste lettergreep, zoowel bij stamwoorden als bij afgeleide woorden. De suffixen worden voor den klemtoon als laatste lettergrepen van het woord waaraan zij gehecht zijn, beschouwd.' Further down the same page: 'In het Wotu'sch schijnt een oxytonisch accent intusschen niet ongewoon te zijn. De Wdl.,…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the word, counting suffixes as part of the word (stress shifts rightward under suffixation, as in Makassarese/Buginese). A minority of words carry final (oxytone) stress; Adriani lists 13 such items from Kruyt's wordlist (aró, ranrá, mitjú, tobó, basó, pitjará, mompodó, mapipí, tabá, marumó, mabaló, molasí, mawarú) and adds (p. 119) that final syllables arising from contraction are also stressed.
new_statements.exceptions: Oxytone words 'not unusual' (13 listed on pp. 118-119); final syllables produced by contraction also take the stress (p. 119, referring to §5). Mead 2013 (fn. 4, p. 8) observes that the words Kruyt marked with final stress are the ones written today with geminate consonants (e.g. mabalô = maballo 'good', tabâ = ? 'wall'), so the 'oxytone' set may reflect pre-geminate prominence rather than lexically free final stress; Adriani himself (p. 119, fn. 4 on maaro) treats the penult as the older position. Grimes & Grimes 1987 (Appendix E) apply the convention 'South Sulawesi stress is penultimate unless marked' to their Wotu list and mark 6 of 52 Wotu rows with a deviating stress apostrophe (ro'u, maga'ya, mopera'ngo, pa'botoa, liye'a, mela ra'ni).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level; explicitly covers stem words and suffixed/derived words (suffix counts as final syllable). Based on a c. 450-item wordlist elicited by Alb. C. Kruyt at Wotu in 1897, not on connected speech; 1898 impressionistic transcription. The only modern description, Mead 2013 (81 pp., itself compiled from Adriani 1898 and two Pusat Bahasa reports), gives no stress rule of its own.
new_statements.identity_note: Adriani 1898 calls the language "Wotu'sch/Wotoe'sch" (title says "To Wadu"), based on a c. 450-item wordlist Kruyt took at Wotu town (Luwu) — the same variety as wotu1240 (no dialects are distinguished in any source). The article's other language, "Sada'sch" (To Sada, described as the southernmost of the Napu-type mountain languages), is a different language and is excluded from the reading.

sources.citation: Grimes, Charles E. & Barbara D. Grimes. 1987. Languages of South Sulawesi. Pacific Linguistics D-78. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Survey-wide convention only (Appendix E, p. 93): 'Stress in South Sulawesi languages usually occurs on the penultimate syllable. In such cases it is not marked in the word lists. Where stress deviates from the normal pattern or where stress may be unclear... it is marked with an apostrophe preceding the stressed syllable.' No Wotu-specific prose; 6 of the 52 Wotu (WOT) word-list rows carry such apostrophes (pp. 97ff.). Open access, hdl 1885/145413.
